title: Lecture 5 – Lacrimal system
html:
Source: c5 lacrimal.pptx – 17 slides

Lacrimal apparatus #1

1. Lacrimal gland #2

  • Diseases
  • Mostly inflammatory diseases
  • dacryoadenites
  • acute
  • chronic

Acute dacryoadenitis #3

  • Causes.
  • infected wounds of the lacrimal gland area
  • often pneumococci and staphylococci
  • less frequently to streptococci.
  • systemic diseases
  • influenza, typhoid fever, mumps
  • Symptoms and signs.
  • swelling and pain
  • temporal half of the upper eyelid
  • free margin distorted (a lying “S” letter).

Acute dacryoadenitis #4

  • Symptoms and signs.
  • swelling and pain
  • temporal half of the upper eyelid
  • free margin distorted(lying “S”)
  • Differential diagnosis:
  • Internal hordeolum (smaller and circumscribed).
  • Eyelid abscess (fluctuation).
  • Orbital cellulitis (usually associated with reduced motility of the eyeball).
  • Management.
  • Treatment
  • Etiological
  • Moist heat, disinfectant compresses (Rivanol), local antibiotics
  • incision and drainage if pus collects

Chronic dacryoadenitis #5

  • Etiology
  • tuberculosis syphilis, leukemia
  • may be the result of an incompletely healed acute dacryoadenitis
  • similarly the condition in Mikulicz syndrome
  • bilateral
  • the sublingual and parotid involved.
  • Symptoms and signs.
  • well circumscribed tumor
  • under the superotemporal orbital margin
  • No pain and local inflammation

Chronic dacryoadenitis #6

  • Management
  • treatment is etiological
  • Systemic corticosteroids may be effective in treating unspecific forms
  • radiation therapy
  • excision of the gland if the inflammation does not recede.

2. Lacrimal drainage system #7

  • Dacryocystitis
  • obstructions of the naso-lacrimal duct
  • stasis within the lacrimal patways
  • saprophyte bacteria (within the tears)
  • inflammation of the mucosa of the lacrimal drainage system
  • congenital and acquired.

Congenital dacryocystitis #8

  • immediately after birth
  • unilateral muco-purulent lacrimation.
  • imperforation of the lower end of the nasolacrimal duct
  • incomplete canalization
  • Differential diagnosis:
  • Gonococcal conjunctivitis and inclusion conjunctivitis
  • Management
  • Topical antibiotics
  • light pressure over lacrimal sac through the lower eyelid
  • reestablishing lacrimal drainage
  • probing the pathways for opening the nasolacrimal duct
  • by about 6 weeks of age.

Congenital dacryocystitis #9

  • After topical anesthetic, the probe is carefully introduced into the lower lacrimal system.
  • The puncta are dilated and then the valve of Hasner is opened (a and b).
  • A dye solution can be introduced to verify patency of the lower lacrimal system (c).
  • In infants six months or older, the procedure is best performed under short-acting general anesthesia.

Acquired dacryocystitis #10

  • Etiopathogeny
  • a) Obstruction of the naso-lacrimal duct
  • causal or surgical traumas,
  • tumors of the face bones,
  • dental inflammation, maxillary sinusitis, rhinitis
  • b) Secondary infection by bacteria
  • from the nasal mucosa and maxillary sinus.

Acquired dacryocystitis #11

  • Symptoms and signs.
  • mostly chronic evolution
  • mucous or mucopurulent discharge
  • parchment like appearance
  • stickiness of the eyelids
  • dilated lacrimal sac
  • tumor like under the direct tendon of the orbicularis muscle
  • disappears by external pressure
  • pus may be expressed into the conjunctival sac

Acquired dacryocystitis #12

  • Differential diagnosis:
  • Hordeolum (small, circumscribed, nonmobile inflamed swelling).
  • Orbital cellulitis (usually associated with reduced motility of the eyeball).

Acquired dacryocystitis #13

  • Management
  • treatment is surgical
  • tear drainage into the nose reestablished by dacryocystorhinostomy
  • anastomosis of the lining of lacrimal sac to the nasal mucosa of the middle meatus after removing the intervening bones.
  • The nasal mucosa and the lacrimal sac are both incised in an H-shapeand door-like flaps are raised.
  • The anterior and posterior mucosal flaps are then sutured together.

Acquired dacryocystitis #14

  • Complication.
  • mucocele of lacrimal sac,
  • blepharoconjunctival inflammation,
  • corneal ulceration,
  • acute dacryocistitis,
  • lacrimal phlegmon.

Acquired dacryocystitis #15

  • Complication.
  • a) Lacrimal sac mucocele
  • by closing openings of the lacrimal sac into conjunctival sac.
  • Treatment
  • Excizion of the lacrimal sac
  • b) Blepharo-conjunctival inflammation
  • due to the pus into conjunctival sac from lacrimal sac.
  • Treatment
  • antiseptics and antibiotics locally

Acquired dacryocystitis #16

  • Complication.
  • c) Corneal ulceration
  • infection of the cornea with bacteria from the lacrimal sac
  • After minimal lesions of the epithelium
  • lubricants, antibiotics and antiseptics locally ;
  • d)Acute dacryocystitis
  • the signs of chronic dacryocystitis,
  • swollen, inflamed and painful lacrimal sac
  • If pus collected, incision and drainage ;

Acquired dacryocystitis #17

  • Complication.
  • e) Lacrimal phlegmon.
  • the bacteria pass trough the surrounding tissues
  • external fistulization of the pus.
  • treatment
  • systemically antibiotics;
  • if pus is collected, incision and drainage ;
  • dacryocystorhinostomy
  • after acute phase,
  • lacrimal drainage restore
